title: Krishna Chooses the Site of Dwaraka
story:
Krishna called the Yadus together in the assembly at Mathura and told them what most of them had been unwilling to say out loud: the city of their birth could not hold them much longer.

"This city is the home of the Yadus," he said. "We were born here and brought up in Vraja. Our griefs have ended and our enemies have been defeated. But our hostilities with the kings have begun, and our battle with Jarasandha has commenced. Our army and our animals are beyond counting, and we have jewels and friends in plenty. Yet Mathura is limited, and an enemy can enter it too easily. If a crore of princes and soldiers live crowded together here, dissension will find its way among them. It is time we laid out a city elsewhere."

The Yadavas heard him out and answered with one delighted voice. "Krishna," they said, "do what you think proper for us all."

When the elders of the Vrishnis consulted among themselves, they spoke of the danger openly. Jarasandha, they said, was destined to be unslayable by them, and his power was very great. Many armies of many kings had been destroyed at Mathura, and still his soldiers were so many that the Yadus could not hope to destroy them even in a hundred years. And then word came that made the decision for them: Jarasandha was marching on Mathura with Kalayavana at his side and a great, irrepressible army behind him.

The Yadus resolved to retreat. Krishna rose in the assembly and said: "Today is an auspicious day. We leave Mathura this very day, with our army and our followers."

They left the city in a flood of gold and dust, headed by Vasudeva, with wives in the chariots and elephants swaying under their burdens, the noise of the column rolling out like the waves of the ocean. They carried their wealth, their kinsmen and their friends; golden chariots, infuriated elephants, horses trotting with gold on their harnesses. They set out toward the west, Vasudeva and the elders guiding the army from the front, and they marched until the ocean rose on the horizon.

The shore they reached was beautiful enough to feel like a reward. It was variegated with creepers, rich in coconut trees, covered with ketaki and palmyras and climbing vines, and the Yadavas looked around them as if they had stepped into a celestial region.

But Krishna had not come there merely to camp. He walked the shore searching for the place where a city could stand, and he found an extensive tract of land on the bank of the ocean. Its soil was coppery and mixed with gravel, well suited for beasts of burden, and it carried every favorable mark a city could want, as if the Goddess of Prosperity herself had chosen to preside over it. The sea breeze fanned it and the ocean watered it. And near it, shining like Mount Mandara, rose the charming mountain Raivata, its slopes rich with gems, a place great men had long resorted to. There the sage Drona had lived for many years, and there the king Ekalavya had dwelt; and on its flank lay a level sporting ground, laid out square like a board of dice, that men called by the name of Dwaravati.

Krishna chose that site for his city. The Yadavas, who had wanted nothing more than to encamp their soldiers there, pitched their tents for the night, and the shore filled with the smoke and voices of a people making themselves at home.

That night Krishna walked among the tents without a trace of anxiety. He thought of the city that would rise on that coppery ground, of the houses that would line its streets and the names he would give them, one by one.

And so the Yadavas secured Dwaravati, and lived there happily with their friends, the way the gods live in their own city: a city still to be built, but already a home.
reflection: Krishna chooses the new city the way a gardener chooses ground, reading the soil, the breeze and the mountain. But he does not seize the land as a conqueror; he puts the proposal to the Yadus first, and the city is founded on their consent as much as on his vision.
tradition_note: The Bhagavata Purana places the founding of Dwaraka after the slaying of Jarasandha. This Harivamsha account, followed here, tells the move differently: the Yadus leave Mathura because Jarasandha and Kalayavana are advancing on the city.
next_story_tease: The tents were barely pitched before Krishna set about making the new city worthy of the name Dwaravati.
hero_scene: Krishna standing on the coppery shore of the western ocean, looking out at the water as the sea breeze lifts his garment, with Mount Raivata rising in the distance behind him and the Yadavas' tents going up along the beach.

coconut and ketaki trees along the coast
